name: Plains Indian Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Berent, Iris and Balaban, Evan and Lennertz, Tracy and Vaknin-Nusbaum, Vered (2010). Phonological Universals Constrain the Processing of Nonspeech Stimuli. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 139. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. pp. 418–435.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The work is about English and Russian speakers' sonority judgments; it describes no signed language and does not concern Plains Indian Sign Language. Catalog has no records for plai1235, so nothing to agree with or contradict.

sources.citation: Tomkins, William. 1929. Universal Indian Sign Language of the Plains Indians of North America (4th ed.). San Diego: the author. (archive.org item bp_985073, scanned text; = Glottolog's Tomkins 1969 Dover reprint 'Indian Sign Language')
sources.note: Nothing on word stress; 'emphasis' only as raising the hand higher / using both hands; 'proper accent' used loosely of fluent signing.

sources.citation: Clark, W. P. 1885. The Indian Sign Language, with brief explanatory notes.. Philadelphia: L. R. Hamersly. (archive.org item cu31924028770570, scanned text)
sources.note: Nothing on word stress; per-sign notes say 'to emphasize, add sign for Brave' or strike more vigorously — gestural intensification only.

sources.citation: Mallery, Garrick. 1881. Sign Language among North American Indians Compared with That among Other Peoples and Deaf-Mutes. First Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology 1879-80, 263-552. Washington: GPO. (Project Gutenberg #17451 text)
sources.note: Nothing on word stress (signed language). Only gestural emphasis: under 'Degrees of comparison' — 'This change in degree of motion is, however, often used for emphasis only, as is the raising of the voice in speech or italicizing and capitalizing in print.'

sources.citation: Davis, Jeffrey E. 2010. Hand Talk: Sign Language among American Indian Nations. Cambridge University Press.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only modern linguistic description of PISL structure (sign phonology, morphology, discourse); would confirm in print that prominence in PISL is gestural/prosodic, if the catalog wants an explicit modality-exclusion citation.

sources.citation: West, La Mont Jr. 1960. The Sign Language: An Analysis. PhD dissertation, Indiana University (2 vols., 307+ pp.).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Glottolog's fullest 'grammar' of PISL; kinemic analysis of sign form. Only relevant if a sign-prosody statement is wanted; contains no spoken stress by nature.

sources.citation: McKay-Cody, Melanie R. 1996. Plains Indian Sign Language: A Comparative Study of Alternate and Primary Signers. (Glottolog lists Indiana University PhD; commonly cited as MA thesis, University of Arizona.)
sources.tag: not read: abstract or record only

sources.citation: Newell, Leonard E. (1981). A stratificational description of Plains Indian Sign Language. Forum Linguisticum 5. pp. 189-212.
sources.access_detail: held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number Philol 17.29); the library holds the journal volume but the item itself was not found; ask your own library for a scan or interlibrary loan
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number Philol 17.29
